entries.note: Marcus reaffirms his own earlier argument. His uncertainty about future importance is not a firm prediction.

entries.test: Public evaluations of contemporary LLMs on novel tasks requiring coherent world models and grounded reasoning would test the categorical claim that they merely combine words without understanding.
entries.note: The categorical functional claim permits empirical testing, although interpreting understanding requires care.

entries.test: Published model architectures, training objectives, and grounding evaluations would establish whether these models only predict contextual words or also connect representations to external-world referents.
entries.note: Predicting words and grounding representations are not necessarily mutually exclusive; evidence must address both parts.
The substantive claim includes Claude's lack of sentience, for which there is no shared evidentiary test. Its functional claims about understanding can be examined separately.

“I don't see an argument” becomes the stronger assertion that no good argument exists. Readers lack a shared test for what constitutes a good argument establishing machine sentience or increased consciousness.

The data explanation is causal and independently testable. The compound claim also strengthens “I don't see” into “there is no good argument” and includes a sentience comparison without a shared test.

entries.test: Public records of Anthropic's acquisition and use of copyrighted works, permissions and licenses, and applicable court findings would establish whether it infringed artists' or writers' rights.
entries.note: In context, this alleges appropriation of protected work, giving the rights claim a concrete factual reading.
“I suspect” explicitly hedges the proposed commercial explanation. The imagined promotional pitch is Marcus's characterization, not an Anthropic quotation.
